title: The Panic That Wasn't
music: Dark, elegant neo-noir orchestral score with a 1930s radio-era colour: muted trumpet, brushed jazz drums, walking upright bass, a faint theremin, piano motif, slow-building tension, a wry quiet resolve at the end, no vocals.
ambience: Faint vintage radio static and distant city rain, no music.

disclosure: Dramatized illustration based on historical records and published research. Images and motion generated with AI (Google Flow: Nano Banana, Veo). Dialogue is quoted from the Radio Guide transcript of Welles's press conference (Oct. 31, 1938) and voiced by synthetic stock voices; no real person's likeness or voice is used.

shots.say: New York. Sunday, October thirtieth, nineteen thirty-eight. Eight o'clock. On CBS radio, a twenty-three-year-old named Orson Welles begins a Halloween play.

sfx.prompt: An old 1930s valve radio warming up, tuning static and a faint dance band fading in

shots.say: It's The War of the Worlds. Martians land on a farm in Grover's Mill, New Jersey. And the story is told as fake news bulletins, breaking into a dance band.

sfx.prompt: Vintage radio crackle and a fireplace in a quiet 1930s living room
Eerie metallic hiss and low rumble from a glowing pit at night

shots.say: By the next morning, America had a legend. It has been told ever since. The trouble is, it's mostly not true.

ov.kicker: THE SIR JACK FILES · SPECIAL EDITION
ov.sub: A true story about a famous false one

sfx.prompt: Huge newspaper printing presses thundering, rhythmic mechanical roar
Deep cinematic boom swelling

shots.say: Monday's New York Times, front page: radio listeners in panic, taking war drama as fact.

sfx.prompt: Rainy 1930s city street at dawn, a newsboy shouting indistinctly, old car horns

shots.say: The papers told of families fleeing their homes, of switchboards jammed with calls.

sfx.prompt: A 1930s car engine racing down a country road at night
Many old telephone bells ringing at once in an office

shots.say: The next day, unshaven, Welles faced the press.

sfx.prompt: Old press camera flashbulbs popping and reporters murmuring in a crowded room

shots.say: A reporter asks:

lines.text: Were you aware of the terror going on throughout the nation while you were giving the broadcast?
Oh no, of course not. I was frankly terribly shocked to learn it did.

sfx.prompt: Reporters murmuring in a crowded smoky room, a flashbulb pop

shots.say: Another:

lines.text: Should you have toned down the language of the drama?
No. You don't play murder in soft words.

sfx.prompt: A single old flashbulb pop and fizz

shots.say: Here's what almost nobody checked. That night, a ratings firm, C. E. Hooper, telephoned five thousand homes and asked what they were listening to.

sfx.prompt: Rotary telephone dialling, then a distant ring

shots.say: Two percent named a radio play, or the Welles show. Not one said a news broadcast.

sfx.prompt: A pencil scratching tally marks on paper, slow

shots.say: Most of America was on NBC, laughing at a ventriloquist and his dummy, Charlie McCarthy. Some CBS stations didn't even carry Welles.

sfx.prompt: 1930s radio studio audience laughing warmly, slightly distant and vintage
An old radio knob clicking and the station changing to static

shots.say: So why the panic headlines? All through the Depression, radio had been taking newspapers' advertisers.

sfx.prompt: 1930s newsroom at night, many typewriters clacking, phones, a ticker

shots.say: Here was proof, the papers said, that radio couldn't be trusted with the news. The Times called it terror by radio.

sfx.prompt: Vintage typewriter typing hard, carriage bell

shots.say: Within a day or two, most papers dropped the story. The legend stayed.

sfx.prompt: Printing presses slowing down and stopping, a long mechanical sigh

shots.say: In nineteen forty, a Princeton study put a number on it: roughly a million frightened. But its survey was taken six weeks later, after the headlines. And frightened is not the same as panicked.

sfx.prompt: A quiet study at night, a slow clock ticking, pages turning

shots.say: Six weeks on, six New York hospitals had no record of a single case. No suicide was ever confirmed.

sfx.prompt: Empty hospital ward at night, distant footsteps echoing, faint wind

shots.say: Nearly fourteen hundred listeners wrote to Welles. Decades later, a historian read their letters. His conclusion: relatively few listeners ever believed the attack was real.

sfx.prompt: Many old paper letters being shuffled and unfolded on a wooden table

shots.say: Washington issued no fines, and no rules. The networks simply promised: no more fake news flashes.

sfx.prompt: Footsteps in a long marble corridor, rain on tall windows

shots.say: But it did happen once. Quito, Ecuador. February twelfth, nineteen forty-nine. Radio Quito airs its own version, set in Ecuador.

sfx.prompt: Night in a hillside city, distant church bell, a radio murmuring indistinctly

shots.say: When listeners learned it was fiction, a crowd stoned the station and set it on fire. People died. Reports put the toll anywhere from five to twenty.

sfx.prompt: Angry crowd shouting, glass breaking, a building on fire roaring
Close crackling roaring fire and falling debris

shots.say: So the most famous panic in history was mostly made in newsrooms. The one that cost lives, almost nobody remembers. A story about fake news that was, itself, mostly fake news. The Sir Jack Files. Case closed.

Single heavy rubber stamp thud on paper on a wooden desk
